title: Walking on the water (Matthew 14:22–33)
hookLine: Peter steps out, looks at the wind, sinks, and a hand catches him
last: WHAT YOU HAND OVER IS ENOUGH.

cards: After the crowd is fed, Jesus sends the disciples ahead across the lake by boat, and goes up a mountain alone to pray. Night falls. Out on the water, the wind is against them, and the boat is tossed by the waves.
Then, in the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, they see someone walking toward them on the water. Matthew says they were troubled and cried out in fear: it's a ghost.

teach.b: Jesus speaks at once, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be of good heart: it is I, fear ye not." It is I. In Greek, two words: egō eimi, I am.
At the burning bush, in the old Greek translation of Exodus, God's name for himself begins with the same two words. Some readers hear that echo here.
Then Peter, being Peter, says: Lord, if it's you, tell me to come to you on the water. Jesus says one word: come. Peter climbs over the side.
And he walks. On the water. Toward Jesus.
Matthew is the one who tells this part.

teach.h: HE SAW THE WIND AND SANK.
teach.b: Then, the text says, Peter saw the wind was strong, and he was afraid, and he began to sink. The wind hadn't changed; it had been strong all night. What changed was where Peter was looking.
As he goes under, he prays: "Lord, save me." Three words. No speech.
And immediately, Matthew says, Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him. The hand was already there. Then, gently: "O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?"
Little faith, not no faith. Peter got out of the boat. The others didn't.

They climb in, the wind stops, and the disciples bow down and say: truly, you are the Son of God. For Catholics, Peter matters especially. He's the one they call the first pope, the rock of the Church.
And here the rock is sinking. The story doesn't hide it. It shows a leader who needed catching, and a hand that caught him.

how: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass, and "Lord, save me" is used as a short prayer in hard moments; Peter's sinking and rescue is often preached as a picture of faith that falters and is caught.

games.q: you're Peter. you've stepped out of the boat and walked on the water. then you notice the wind. what happens?
o: you keep walking without a pause.
you're afraid, you start to sink, and you cry out.
you turn around and climb back into the boat.
games.why: he begins to sink and cries, “Lord, save me.” immediately a hand catches him: “O thou of little faith, why didst thou doubt?”

practice: Where in your life are you looking at the wind: a money worry, a health scare, a relationship that feels like deep water? Name it plainly, inside, and notice whether you've already stepped out, already started trying.
If you pray, you can say Peter's three words, Lord, save me, and picture the hand reaching out; if not, just notice where you're looking, and try looking a little further up.

wordCard.voice: egō eimi. I am, the words Jesus spoke on the water, echoing God's own name at the burning bush.

orig.note: Greek: I am, or it is I. Jesus's words on the water; some readers hear in them God's name at the burning bush.
